transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Carlos (CISO), Lena (Infra), Ibrahim (Sec Eng), Priya (Compliance)

Summary:
High-level security review focused on encryption at rest/in transit, BYOK integration, HSM connector validation, and regulatory data residency requirements for Stratus Energy. Agreement to run a short lab validation, exchange runbook and SOW, and confirm approved HSM vendors and regions. Some questions around separation of duties and audit log granularity remain.

Topics covered:
- Encryption at rest model: envelope encryption, key wrapping, and KMS vs customer-managed HSM
- In-transit encryption: TLS mTLS between services and internal traffic flow
- BYOK workflow: key import vs key wrap, key material lifecycle, rotation and emergency key rollover
- HSM connector options: cloud HSM vs on-prem HSM appliance, offline signing, PKCS#11 support
- Auditability: cryptographic event logs, key usage metrics, and integration with Splunk/SIEM
- Separation of duties & role-based access controls for key operations
- Data residency mapping and pilot scope

Action items (spoken in call):
- Maya: will assemble a BYOK/HSM runbook and example API calls (putKey, wrapKey)
- Jordan: share pilot SOW and draft SLA appendix re: key custody and uptime guarantees
- Carlos: return list of allowed regions and HSM vendors to test against

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: "All right, everyone, thanks for joining, we can do quick intros. I'm Jordan, I'm the AE for Stratus, and with me is Maya, our security engineer who owns the BYOK and HSM integrations."
[00:17] Carlos: "Hey, thanks. I'm Carlos, CISO at Stratus Energy — we run the infrastructure in a mix of cloud regions and a couple of on-prem data centres. We're especially worried about keys leaving our control and about auditability for SOC 2."
[00:32] Maya: "Great, thanks Carlos. Today we can talk through how Redwood supports BYOK, HSM connectors, and the audit/logging surface you can expect. I might jump into some architecture diagrams, I shared a short deck in the calendar invite."
[00:47] Lena: "Quickly, we have two requirements: 1) keys never persist unwrapped outside our KMS/HSM, and 2) we need to prove separation of duties — infra can't rotate keys by themselves, ops needs approval."
[01:05] Maya: "Yep, that's consistent with envelope encryption — Redwood can accept wrapped key material and then perform tokenized operations. We support a key-wrapping flow where your KMS acts as the root, and we never have the plaintext key material persisted in our control plane. There are two patterns: import key material into our KMS (we support import-wrapped keys) or we hold a wrapped key and call your HSM for unwrap/crypto ops via connector."
[01:33] Ibrahim: "When you say 'connector' — is that over a mTLS tunnel? Is it a push model or pull? We prefer a pull model where we have control of the HSM endpoint."
[01:44] Maya: "Good question. Our typical connector does a mutual TLS session initiated from a Redwood appliance in the customer's VPC to your HSM gateway, so it's outbound from your network. We also support VPN-based connectivity and on-prem forwarding for customers who need no inbound access. The connection supports PKCS#11 or a REST shim for cloud HSMs."
[02:10] Priya: "Does that mean the key operations (sign/decrypt) can happen entirely inside our HSM and Redwood only gets the ciphertext response?"
[02:18] Maya: "Yes, correct. If you use the 'remote-operation' mode, Redwood will send the ciphertext to your HSM via the connector, the HSM handles the decryption/signing and returns the result — we never see raw key material. The trade-off is added network latency per op, but for many workloads this is within acceptable bounds; for low-latency inference you can instead provision a cached wrapped key in a secure enclave with limited time-to-live."
[02:45] Carlos: "Latency numbers would be helpful. Also, we will need to prove to our SOC 2 auditor that key usage logs show identity of the caller, timestamp, and operation — basically full audit trace."
[02:58] Maya: "Absolutely. Redwood emits cryptographic audit events: key_id, caller_token, action (encrypt/decrypt/sign), bytes processed, and a correlation_id. We can route those logs to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) via syslog or an S3 delivery. We keep an internal immutable ledger for key operations too, which we can export as part of an auditor bundle."
[03:20] Ibrahim: "Is the ledger tamper-evident? We prefer something append-only with checksums or Merkle history for forensic purposes."
[03:29] Maya: "Right now we have HMAC-chained event records which are tamper-evident for the retention window. We're working on a Merkle-based export for high-assurance customers — I can put that on the roadmap. For your audit timeframe, we can provide signed bundles with HMACs and timestamps."
[03:48] Lena: "On rotation — we need to rotate keys quarterly and have emergency rollovers. Can Redwood orchestrate rotation with our HSM so that new keys are generated in our HSM and rotated into service without downtime?"
[04:03] Maya: "Yes — we support orchestrated rotation. The most conservative pattern is: generate a new key in your HSM, export the wrapped key material to Redwood, Redwood verifies the wrap and switches traffic, we keep the previous key for a rollover window. For emergency rollover, we have a fallback policy that can instruct traffic to a warmed fallback model or to another region — depends on your SLO."
[04:25] Carlos: "If we rotate in our HSM, do we need to share the private key with Redwood?"
[04:31] Maya: "No. You can generate the key in your HSM and provide a wrapped version or allow remote ops. If you allow remote ops, we never see the private key. If you deliver wrapped key material, Redwood will only persist wrapped payloads and never the unwrapped key."
[04:47] Jordan: "Two quick commercial notes — for dedicated instances we can offer a per-tenant isolated runtime so the keys are associated with a tenant-specific keystore and access controls. For private deployments we can also install the connector appliance inside your VPC for complete egress control."
[05:05] Carlos: "Good. On vendors, we have YubiHSM and Gemalto appliances internally; we also evaluate cloud HSM from the major clouds. Any constraints?"
[05:15] Maya: "We support PKCS#11-compatible HSMs and have successfully integrated with YubiHSM and Thales/Gemalto. For some vendors there’s a small adapter required — we have an open connector shim that your infra team can run behind a bastion. We test for FIPS 140-2 compliance on the path."
[05:33] Ibrahim: "About separation of duties — where does Redwood log admin actions like key import, policy changes, and role grants? We need separate audit trails for ops and security teams."
[05:44] Maya: "We log admin API calls separately from per-operation cryptographic events. Admin logs include the actor, IP, session token, and action (createKey, importKey, setPolicy). Those can be exported to your SIEM with role tags. For RBAC, there's integration with your SSO (SAML/SCIM) so admin roles map to your identity provider groups. So change events will contain the SSO identity in the audit log."
[06:12] Priya: "Does Redwood support MFA for privileged key ops?"
[06:16] Maya: "We can require step-up authentication for certain operations; currently that ties to your IdP's policies. We also support manual approval flows for key import or emergency rollover, where a second approver must sign off — that meets separation-of-duties requirements."
[06:32] Carlos: "Can you show, at a high level, how the data residency mapping will look? We have EU, US, and a Canada region with specific sovereignty needs."
[06:41] Jordan: "Sure — I pulled up a quick map. Redwood can pin keys to region-specific keystores, and routing policies ensure inference requests hitting EU datasets use EU-hosted model shards and keystores. We also support a strict residency mode where no key material leaves the region — that is implemented via connectors to on-region HSMs."
[07:05] Lena: "What about backups and escrow — do we have to escrow keys with a third party?"
[07:10] Maya: "We don't require escrow but offer an optional key escrow service if you want a third-party recovery option. The escrow bundle can be encrypted under an escrow key that's split using Shamir's Secret Sharing if you want multi-party custody. Many customers opt to hold escrow externally with their legal custodian."
[07:29] Ibrahim: "Auditor stuff — what artifacts do you provide for SOC 2?"
[07:34] Maya: "We provide the standard SOC 2 audit pack, plus specific crypto artifacts: KMS architecture diagram, connector design, sample audit log extracts, rotation policies, and attestation around HSM FIPS level. We can also sign an appendix to the SOC 2 report describing your BYOK setup."
[07:54] Priya: "If the auditor needs to replay events, can we provide an ordered event stream?"
[07:58] Maya: "Yes, we can provide an ordered export of events for the retention window; we sign the export and include hashing to prove integrity."
[08:07] Carlos: "One risk: how do we handle key destruction requests for e-discovery or regulatory takedown?"
[08:14] Maya: "We support certified key destruction workflows. If you issue a destruction command, we mark the key as revoked, rotate it out of service, and — depending on the deployment — either instruct your HSM to destroy key material or delete wrapped material in Redwood and produce a destruction certificate."
[08:34] Lena: "Do you provide destruction certificates? We need that for compliance."
[08:37] Maya: "Yes, we issue a signed certificate with timestamp and attestation of the operation. For HSM-based keys, the HSM vendor may also provide a separate audit of the erase procedure."
[08:49] Jordan: "Back to practical next steps — Maya, can you run a 2-hour lab test with the Stratus infra team where we validate PKCS#11 ops, key import, and the audit log export?"
[08:58] Maya: "Yes, I suggest a 2-hour window: we will validate connector set-up, run a few encrypt/decrypt ops, rotate a key, and then request an audit export. We'll capture latency and show instrumentation. I can prepare a checklist."
[09:12] Ibrahim: "That works. Week of 6/29 is good for us, any day after Tuesday preferred."
[09:19] Carlos: "One more question on emergency access: if Stratus infra team is unreachable, does Redwood have a break-glass mechanism?"
[09:26] Maya: "We have a controlled emergency access flow that requires >=2 approvers from your organization plus Redwood's on-call security to execute a break-glass. The operation is logged and requires justification. For private deployments you can also disable break-glass by policy if you want absolute denial."
[09:45] Priya: "We'd like the break-glass flow documented and the list of Redwood on-call contacts for our records."
[09:50] Jordan: "We'll include a break-glass appendix in the SOW and provide the on-call roster under NDA."
[09:58] Carlos: "Sounds good. Anything else?"
[10:01] Jordan: "I'll note two open items: 1) Maya to produce runbook and lab checklist; 2) Jordan to send SOW and draft SLA appendix; 3) Carlos to send vendor/region list. If that aligns we can reconvene after the lab."
[10:14] Lena: "Yep, confirmed."
[10:16] Carlos: "Thanks, everyone."
[10:18] Jordan: "Thanks all — we'll follow up by email with links. I'll drop the security docs and runbook link: https://redwood.example.com/security/stratus-byo-runbook (draft)."
[10:32] (end of recorded segment — remaining minutes used for informal Q&A and scheduling)

Notes on transcription quality: some speaker labels conflated (e.g., Infra vs Ibrahim in a few short segments), occasional word swaps (e.g., 'shard' recognized as 'shard' vs 'short') — audio was clear overall.
